title: Delta Lake internals & table optimization
objectives: Capture a defensible BASELINE for two project tables (silver_pricing, gold_price_integrity_mart): record file count, median/percentile file size, total bytes, and the wall-clock + bytes-scanned of one representative Maria query read straight from the Spark UI / query profile — before changing anything.

Apply OPTIMIZE bin-packing AND liquid clustering keyed to the ACTUAL query predicates (e.g. CLUSTER BY payer_id, hospital_ccn, billing_code) and quantify the result as files pruned, bytes scanned, and runtime delta on the same benchmark query.

Decide partition-vs-cluster for each table using the small-files-trap rule (partition only low-cardinality columns yielding >~1 GB per partition; otherwise cluster) and justify the choice in one written paragraph per table.

Configure VACUUM with a defensible retention window and prove clean recovery: simulate a bad MERGE, then restore the table with RESTORE / VERSION AS OF and confirm row counts match the pre-incident version.

Open the Performance Notes README section with a before/after table that LEADS WITH THE BUSINESS OUTCOME (report lands before Maria's 8am review; ~X% fewer bytes scanned = lower DBU) not the technical change.
lessons: Delta file layout internals: the _delta_log transaction log (JSON commits + checkpoints), Parquet data files, add/remove actions, and how a snapshot is reconstructed. Why thousands of tiny files (the streaming/Auto Loader side effect from Phase 3) inflate metadata and driver time and starve executors. (~1.0h)

MEASURE FIRST tooling: reading the Spark UI stages and the SQL query profile, DESCRIBE DETAIL / DESCRIBE HISTORY, per-file min/max data-skipping stats, and how to isolate the ONE slow stage before touching a single knob. (~1.0h)

OPTIMIZE (bin-packing compaction) vs liquid clustering vs legacy Z-ORDER: what each physically does, why clustering keys must follow the QUERY PATTERN (Maria filters by payer and hospital) not the data model, and why liquid clustering is now the default over partition+Z-order. (~1.25h)

Partitioning tradeoffs and the small-files trap: cardinality math, the >~1 GB-per-partition rule of thumb, why partitioning billing_code or npi is a foot-gun, and migrating a badly-partitioned table to clustering. (~0.75h)

VACUUM, retention, and time travel for recovery: how remove actions become tombstones, the default 7-day retention and why shrinking it can break concurrent readers/time travel, RESTORE vs VERSION AS OF, and pairing recovery with an audit-log entry. (~0.75h)
Predictive optimization / auto-tuning: when Databricks manages OPTIMIZE + VACUUM for you and when a human should still hand-tune and record the decision. (~0.25h)
businessFraming: Maria's price-integrity mart now backs a daily 8am revenue-cycle review, but since Phase 3 turned the pipeline to streaming, Auto Loader is dribbling thousands of tiny Delta files into silver_pricing and the mart query has crept past the deadline — every late report is a payer-dispute review that slips a day and a chargemaster correction that ages. Slow, bloated tables are also a direct DBU bill: every needless byte scanned is money. This week we make the tables fast and cheap without changing a single business rule, and we prove the win with numbers.
labSummary: Working entirely on the running project's OWN Delta tables (no new raw data), you measure a baseline, tune silver_pricing and gold_price_integrity_mart by query pattern, resolve the small-files trap left by streaming ingestion, set VACUUM + retention, rehearse a time-travel recovery, and open the Performance Notes section with a business-led before/after. Every step is 'measure first, change one thing, measure again.'
labSteps: BASELINE (measure first): on silver_pricing and gold_price_integrity_mart run DESCRIBE DETAIL (numFiles, sizeInBytes) and DESCRIBE HISTORY; run one representative Maria query (e.g. price integrity for a given payer_id + hospital_ccn) with a cold cache and record wall-clock, bytes scanned, and files read from the SQL query profile. Screenshot the slow stage in the Spark UI. Paste all numbers into a baseline block — you cannot claim a win without this.

Diagnose the small-files trap: quantify median file size and file count growth from streaming writes. Confirm from the query profile whether the slow stage is scan/IO (too many small files, weak data skipping) vs shuffle/skew — do NOT fix what isn't slow.

Compact with OPTIMIZE (bin-packing) on the worst table, then re-run DESCRIBE DETAIL and the benchmark query; record the new file count/size and runtime. Note the delta before adding clustering so you can attribute each gain.

Add liquid clustering keyed to the QUERY PATTERN: ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (payer_id, hospital_ccn, billing_code) chosen from Maria's actual filters, then OPTIMIZE to realize the layout. Re-run the benchmark; record files pruned and bytes scanned vs baseline. Contrast with what naive partitioning by billing_code would have done (compute the resulting partition/file count on paper).

Decide and document partition-vs-cluster per table using the >~1 GB-per-partition rule; write one paragraph each justifying why you clustered (or, for a genuinely low-cardinality column like ingest_date, partitioned). This written 'why' is an interview answer.

Set retention + VACUUM: choose a defensible retention window (default 7 days; justify any change), run VACUUM in DRY RUN first, then for real, and note reclaimed bytes. Explain in the runbook how shortening retention would break time travel / concurrent readers.

Rehearse recovery (build for failure): simulate a bad write (e.g. a MERGE that overwrites prices with nulls), detect it, then recover with RESTORE TABLE ... TO VERSION AS OF the last-good version; confirm row counts and a spot-checked price match pre-incident, and write an audit-log row (table, bad version, restored version, timestamp, why).
Sanity-check idempotency isn't broken: re-run the streaming/incremental load once after tuning to confirm OPTIMIZE/clustering didn't change results, only layout.

Write the Performance Notes section: a before/after table (files, bytes scanned, runtime, est. DBU) with a one-line headline LEADING WITH THE BUSINESS OUTCOME ('mart now lands ~4 min, comfortably before the 8am review; ~55% fewer bytes scanned'), then the technical changes underneath.

title: Databricks & Unity Catalog — governing the project
objectives: Design a three-level Unity Catalog namespace (catalog.schema.table) that maps to the bronze/silver/gold medallion layers, and write a one-paragraph justification for the chosen boundary (single project catalog with per-layer schemas vs. per-layer catalogs).

For every table in the running Provider Pricing Integrity project, make an explicit managed-vs-external decision and defend it in a table, then register/migrate the tables so 100% resolve under the new UC namespace (verified via information_schema.tables).

Implement least-privilege RBAC with GRANT/REVOKE for at least 3 personas (data engineer, analyst 'Maria', compliance auditor) and prove enforcement with a denied-then-granted access test captured as evidence.

Apply governance tags (e.g., pii, phi_adjacent, medallion_layer, data_owner, cost_center) to catalog/schema/table/column objects and query them back through system tables to prove they are machine-discoverable, not just comments.
Capture built-in column-level lineage for the CMS pricing -> silver -> gold KPI path and export it (screenshot + system.access lineage query) into the Architecture Doc as governance evidence.
lessons: Unity Catalog architecture: the metastore, the three-level namespace (catalog -> schema -> table), how UC supersedes the legacy hive_metastore and default DBFS, and account-level vs workspace-level identity. Why a governance layer exists at all for PHI-adjacent data.

Managed vs external tables: where bytes live, managed storage locations/credentials & external locations, DROP TABLE semantics (managed = data deleted, external = metadata only), who owns VACUUM/retention, and the decision rule for each medallion layer.

The securable-object privilege model: USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA gating, SELECT/MODIFY/BROWSE, object ownership, why you GRANT to groups not users, and how privilege inheritance flows down the namespace.

Attribute-based governance with tags, plus a first look at column masks / row filters as the compliance hook for next phases (introduced, not fully built) — how tags make 'find every PHI-adjacent column' a query instead of a meeting.
Built-in lineage and auditability: table & column lineage, the lineage graph UI, and reading system tables (system.access.*, information_schema) so ownership and access are provable to an auditor.
businessFraming: Maria's provider-pricing tables currently live in the default hive_metastore with no owner, no access control, and no PHI tagging — meaning provider names, addresses, and competitively-sensitive negotiated rates are readable by anyone on the workspace and untraceable in an audit. For PHI-adjacent data that is a real compliance exposure (and a failed audit is real money): this week converts 'a pipeline that works' into 'a pipeline a compliance officer will sign off on' by putting the whole project under governed, least-privilege, lineage-tracked access.
labSummary: Retrofit the entire Phase 2 Provider Pricing Integrity project into Unity Catalog: design and stand up the catalog/schema structure per medallion layer, make and document a managed-vs-external decision per table, migrate the tables, lock them down with persona-based GRANTs, tag PHI-adjacent columns, and capture built-in lineage as audit evidence. No new raw data — you are governing the project you already built.
labSteps: DESIGN FIRST (on paper, before any SQL): sketch the target namespace. Decide one project catalog (e.g. ppi_prod) with schemas bronze/silver/gold/ops, OR per-layer catalogs — and write 3-4 sentences on why, tied to how Maria's analysts vs engineers query. Draft a managed-vs-external decision table with one row per project table and a reason column.

Stand up the structure with a parameterized notebook: CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS, then CREATE SCHEMA per layer, plus MANAGED LOCATION / an external location + storage credential for any layer you decided to keep external. Set COMMENT and OWNER (a group, not you) on each object.

Migrate the Phase 2 tables into UC. For managed targets use CREATE TABLE ... DEEP CLONE or CTAS from the old hive_metastore tables; for external, register with CREATE TABLE ... LOCATION. Verify with SELECT * FROM information_schema.tables that every project table resolves under the new namespace and count = expected.

Implement RBAC for 3 personas via groups: GRANT USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA + SELECT on gold to an analysts group (Maria), MODIFY on bronze/silver to an engineers group, and read-only + BROWSE to an auditors group. Keep it least-privilege — no blanket ALL PRIVILEGES.

Prove enforcement: as (or simulating) the analyst persona, run a SELECT on a silver table you did NOT grant and capture the permission-denied error; then GRANT the minimum needed and re-run to success. Save both outputs — this denied-then-granted pair is your interview evidence.

Capture lineage: run the silver->gold KPI transformation once under UC so lineage populates, open the lineage graph for a gold KPI table, screenshot the column-level path from CMS pricing fields, and run a system.access lineage query to export the same as a table.

DOCUMENT: update the Architecture Doc with the final namespace diagram, the managed-vs-external decision table, the GRANT matrix, the tag taxonomy, and the lineage screenshot. Write a short 'why' note: why this catalog boundary, why groups over users, why external for the layer(s) you chose. Idempotency check: re-run the setup notebook end-to-end and confirm it is safe (IF NOT EXISTS / no errors) on the 2nd and 3rd run.

title: Declarative pipelines I — Lakeflow/DLT with expectations
objectives: Rebuild the Phase 2 bronze→silver pipeline as a DECLARATIVE Lakeflow pipeline: define at least 2 streaming tables (bronze CMS pricing ingest, silver validated providers) and at least 1 materialized view (a conformed KPI-ready view) using @dlt decorators, and successfully run a full + incremental update with zero manual notebook orchestration.

Encode the W28 data-quality rules as EXPECTATIONS-as-code using all three enforcement tiers — expect (warn/track), expect_or_drop (quarantine), expect_or_fail (halt) — with at least 6 named expectations covering pricing completeness, NPI format, non-null grain keys, and valid negotiated-rate ranges.
Read the Lakeflow pipeline's automatic LINEAGE graph and the per-expectation data-quality metrics from the event log, and record the pass/drop/fail counts per named expectation for one update run.

Justify each expectation's tier choice in writing (why a bad NPI drops to quarantine but a missing grain key fails the run), tying each decision to Maria's revenue-cycle risk so the rule set reads as governance, not decoration.

Query the pipeline event log (system table / event_log TVF) to extract data-quality metrics and expectation results, proving the pipeline observes and reports quality rather than silently passing bad rows.
lessons: What 'declarative' means and why it matters here: contrast the Phase 2 imperative notebook (you write the read→transform→write→checkpoint→merge orchestration by hand) with Lakeflow declarative pipelines where you DECLARE the target tables and their queries and the runtime infers dependencies, execution order, incremental vs. full refresh, and checkpoint management. Map the medallion project onto streaming tables (append/incremental ingest) vs. materialized views (recomputed conformed/aggregated outputs) and state the decision rule for which to use. (~1.25 hr)

Streaming tables vs. materialized views vs. views in Lakeflow: semantics of each, when incremental refresh is possible, the cost/freshness tradeoff, and how Auto Loader (cloud_files) feeds a streaming table — framed as the on-ramp to the W34/W35 continuous story without building orchestration or full streaming yet. (~1.25 hr)

Expectations as data contracts: the three tiers — expect (retain + warn/track), expect_or_drop (drop row + record), expect_or_fail (stop the update) — their exact runtime behavior, how each is counted in the event log, and the design principle 'break safely, loud not silent' applied to each tier. Includes @dlt.expect_all / expect_all_or_drop for grouping rules. (~1.5 hr)

Migrating the W28 DQ rules into expectations: translate each existing rule (pricing-completeness, NPI 10-digit checksum-shaped format, non-null grain composite key, negotiated-rate plausibility bounds, duplicate-provider signal) into a named boolean constraint, and decide its tier by business consequence to Maria — the core governance judgment of the week. (~1.0 hr)

Automatic lineage and the pipeline event log: how Lakeflow captures column/table lineage in Unity Catalog (building on W32), and how to read data-quality metrics, expectation pass/drop/fail counts, and update status from the event log via the event_log TVF / pipeline system tables — this is your observability and interview evidence. (~1.0 hr)

Anti-pattern guardrails: keeping the pipeline as a small, human-readable set of table definitions — NOT an over-modularized maze of tiny files. When to use one notebook of clear @dlt functions vs. splitting; why over-engineering the pipeline is a trap and how a reviewer spots a human-authored, intentional rule set. (~0.5 hr)
businessFraming: Maria's revenue-cycle team stopped trusting the pricing dataset after a silent bad-load pushed negotiated rates that were off by orders of magnitude into a payer-contract review — the notebook pipeline ran green while shipping garbage. A hospital that publishes or negotiates on wrong transparency data faces both CMS compliance exposure and real dollars left on the table in contract talks. This week converts the pipeline from 'ran without erroring' to 'provably enforced its data contract on every row,' so a bad negotiated rate or malformed NPI is caught, quarantined, and reported before it can reach a contract decision.
labSummary: Convert the Phase 2 bronze→silver stage of the Provider Pricing Integrity pipeline into a declarative Lakeflow pipeline in your Unity Catalog (from W32), with the W28 DQ rules re-expressed as named, tiered expectations. You will define streaming tables for CMS pricing ingest and silver validated providers, a materialized view for a conformed KPI-ready output, run a full and then an incremental update, and then read lineage plus per-expectation quality metrics from the event log — recording pass/drop/fail counts and writing the 'why this tier' justification for each rule.
labSteps: SETUP & FRAME: In your project repo, create a new pipeline source notebook/file (e.g. pipelines/silver_pricing.py). Open it with a 1–2 sentence business-framing comment naming Maria and the contract-decision risk. Confirm your W32 Unity Catalog + schema (catalog.schema) and the UC Volume landing path where raw CMS pricing files arrive — you target UC, not hive_metastore.

DECLARE BRONZE STREAMING TABLE: Using the starter scaffold, define an Auto Loader (cloud_files) streaming table that ingests the raw CMS Hospital Price Transparency files into bronze as append-only with ingest metadata (source file, ingest timestamp) — no business logic. Run a first pipeline full-refresh update and confirm bronze populates.

TRANSLATE THE W28 RULES: In a markdown cell, list your existing W28 DQ rules and, next to each, write the boolean constraint expression and the chosen tier. Minimum 6: pricing-completeness (rate present), NPI 10-digit format, non-null grain composite key (provider+code+payer), negotiated-rate plausibility bounds (>0 and < a sane ceiling), payer/plan not-null, and a stale-file freshness flag. This is a design table you will defend.

DEFINE SILVER STREAMING TABLE WITH EXPECTATIONS: Build the silver validated_pricing streaming table reading from bronze (dlt.read_stream) and apply your expectations: @dlt.expect_or_fail on the non-null grain key (unrecoverable — halt), @dlt.expect_or_drop on bad NPI and implausible rates (quarantine, not golden path), and @dlt.expect (warn/track) on soft-completeness signals. Type/conform columns as in Phase 2.

ADD THE MATERIALIZED VIEW: Define a materialized view that conforms silver into a KPI-ready shape (one clean row per grain with cleaned rate + provider attributes) — the input your Phase 2 gold marts will later consume. Comment WHY this is a materialized view (recomputed conformed output) while the two silver tables are streaming (incremental append ingest).

RUN FULL + INCREMENTAL: Trigger a full pipeline update; confirm the lineage/DAG renders and all three tables build in inferred dependency order. Then drop ONE new/changed CMS file into the landing path and run an incremental update — confirm only new data flows through and the streaming tables append without reprocessing everything.

READ QUALITY METRICS + LINEAGE: Query the pipeline event log (event_log TVF or the pipeline system table) to pull per-expectation results for your latest update; record passing/dropped/failing counts per named expectation into a results table in the notebook/Runbook. Then open the UC lineage for the materialized view and confirm column-level lineage traces back through silver to bronze to the source files (ties to W32); capture it as governance evidence.

FORCE A FAILURE ON PURPOSE (break-safely proof): Introduce a row with a null grain key (or point at a deliberately corrupt test file) and run an update; confirm the expect_or_fail expectation HALTS the update loudly rather than passing. Then confirm a bad-NPI row is DROPPED (not failed) and shows in the drop count. Revert. This proves loud-not-silent behavior for the interview.

WRITE THE 'WHY' NOTE: In the architecture doc, add a 'Data Contract' subsection: for each expectation, one line stating the rule, its tier, and the Maria-facing consequence that justifies the tier (e.g. 'missing grain key → fail: a row with no key can't be deduped or trusted in a contract review'). Add the event-log pass/drop/fail numbers as the observability evidence.

# Provider Pricing Integrity — Silver stage as a declarative Lakeflow pipeline
# BUSINESS FRAMING: Maria's team makes payer-contract decisions on this data.
# A silent bad load = wrong negotiated rates in a contract review. This pipeline
# must ENFORCE and REPORT its data contract on every row, not just "run green."
#
# NOTE: configure catalog/schema in the pipeline settings (target your W32 UC),
# and set the CMS landing path as a pipeline parameter. Do NOT hardcode secrets.

import dlt
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, current_timestamp, input_file_name

# CMS raw file landing location (set via pipeline config / spark conf)
# TODO: read this from a pipeline parameter, not a literal
CMS_LANDING_PATH = spark.conf.get("pricing.landing_path", "/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/landing/cms_pricing")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) BRONZE — streaming ingest of raw CMS pricing files via Auto Loader
#    Append-only. NO business logic here. Keep it thin.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
@dlt.table(
    name="bronze_cms_pricing",
    comment="Raw CMS Hospital Price Transparency files, append-only via Auto Loader.",
)
def bronze_cms_pricing():
    return (
        spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")
        .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv")  # TODO: confirm real format per file drop
        # TODO: add schema hints / schemaLocation; CMS files are inconsistent
        .load(CMS_LANDING_PATH)
        .withColumn("_ingest_ts", current_timestamp())
        .withColumn("_source_file", input_file_name())
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) SILVER — validated, typed, conformed pricing as a STREAMING table
#    This is where the W28 rules become tiered expectations.
#    Tier guide: expect = warn/track | expect_or_drop = quarantine
#                expect_or_fail = halt the update (unrecoverable)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
@dlt.table(
    name="silver_validated_pricing",
    comment="Typed, conformed pricing with enforced data contract.",
)
# HARD FAIL — a row with no grain key cannot be deduped or trusted downstream.
# TODO: replace with your real composite-grain null check (provider+code+payer)
@dlt.expect_or_fail("grain_key_present", "provider_npi IS NOT NULL AND code IS NOT NULL AND payer IS NOT NULL")
# QUARANTINE — malformed NPI: drop from golden path, count it, don't kill the run.
# TODO: tighten to your real 10-digit NPI shape rule from W28
@dlt.expect_or_drop("npi_10_digit", "provider_npi RLIKE '^[0-9]{10}$'")
# QUARANTINE — implausible negotiated rate.
# TODO: set the sane ceiling you justified in W28
@dlt.expect_or_drop("rate_in_bounds", "negotiated_rate > 0 AND negotiated_rate < 1000000")
# WARN/TRACK — soft completeness signal you measure but do not enforce.
@dlt.expect("payer_plan_present", "payer IS NOT NULL AND plan IS NOT NULL")
# TODO: add at least 2 more named expectations to reach your >=6 rule contract
def silver_validated_pricing():
    df = dlt.read_stream("bronze_cms_pricing")
    # TODO: cast/clean columns to typed schema (rate -> decimal, trim codes, etc.)
    # TODO: conform CMS column-name variants to your canonical silver schema
    # TODO: derive provider_npi / code / payer / plan / negotiated_rate
    return df


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3) MATERIALIZED VIEW — conformed, KPI-ready output for the (later) gold marts.
#    Materialized view because it is a RECOMPUTED conformed output, not an
#    incremental append. Downstream Phase 2 gold marts will read this.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
@dlt.table(
    name="silver_pricing_conformed_mv",
    comment="One clean row per grain, KPI-ready. Feeds gold marts.",
)
def silver_pricing_conformed_mv():
    # TODO: dedupe to one row per composite grain + select KPI-facing columns
    return dlt.read("silver_validated_pricing")


# AFTER RUNNING: query the event log for per-expectation pass/drop/fail counts
# and paste them into the Runbook. TODO: add your event_log TVF query here or in
# a companion notebook.

Failing the whole update on a recoverable row-level defect (a bad NPI) is worse operations, not better — it takes the pipeline down instead of quarantining one row. Strictness is a per-rule business decision, not a global setting.

title: Declarative pipelines II — Jobs & orchestration
objectives: Assemble the running project into ONE multi-task Databricks Job DAG: a Lakeflow pipeline task → MDM golden-record refresh task → gold marts/KPI refresh task, with explicit upstream dependencies and a run-if gate on the final task.

Configure task-level retries (with min-retry-interval), a per-task timeout, and max-concurrent-runs=1 so a slow run never stacks on top of itself; verify by triggering a forced failure and watching the automatic retry.
Parameterize the job: pass a job-level `run_date` and `env` parameter down into the pipeline and MDM tasks, and read them at runtime (no hard-coded dates/paths).
Wire failure + duration-SLA notifications: on-failure alert to email/webhook AND an on-duration-threshold-exceeded alert that fires when the run misses the 8am freshness SLA.

Prove safe recovery: kill the job mid-DAG, use Repair Run to resume from the failed task only, and confirm a full rerun is idempotent by running the job 10x and showing gold row counts/KPIs are stable.
lessons: Databricks Jobs anatomy for a real DAG: tasks and task types (Lakeflow **pipeline** task vs notebook vs SQL task), `depends_on` edges, serverless vs job compute, and why the medallion pipeline should be several dependent tasks instead of one mega-notebook. (~50 min)

Reliability controls: `max_retries` + `min_retry_interval_millis`, task `timeout_seconds`, `max_concurrent_runs`, and `run_if` conditions (ALL_SUCCESS vs AT_LEAST_ONE_FAILED) so the pipeline breaks LOUD and recovers cleanly, not silently. (~45 min)
Passing state through the DAG: job parameters vs task parameters, and `taskValues` (dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set/get) to hand a computed batch id / row count from one task to the next. (~40 min)

Scheduling & triggers: cron/quartz schedules, timezone + pause toggle, and continuous vs triggered — we stay on a SCHEDULED trigger this week (file-arrival/Auto Loader streaming is W35, not now). (~35 min)

Notifications & operational SLAs: on-start/on-success/on-failure destinations, system notification destinations (email/Slack/PagerDuty webhook), and the on-duration-threshold-exceeded alert as the freshness-SLA tripwire. (~40 min)

Recovery mechanics: Repair Run (rerun only failed/downstream tasks), why every task must be idempotent for repair to be safe, and reading the run timeline/Gantt to find the critical-path task. (~30 min)
businessFraming: Maria's revenue-cycle team pulls the pricing-integrity report at 8:00am to flag providers billing outside the CMS-published rate; if the MDM golden-record step silently fails but the gold marts still refresh off yesterday's data, Maria bills against duplicated/stale providers — a compliance and cash-recovery exposure. A single orchestrated Job with dependencies, retries, and a freshness-SLA alert turns "did the pipeline run last night?" from a morning fire-drill into a page that either says all-clear or tells you exactly which task broke and when.
labSummary: Take the Phase 2 medallion pipeline (Lakeflow declarative pipeline from W33 + MDM golden refresh + gold marts/KPIs) and orchestrate it as one production multi-task Databricks Job DAG. Add task dependencies, retries, timeouts, parameters, a cron schedule, and both failure and freshness-SLA notifications — then deliberately break it and recover with Repair Run, and prove idempotency across 10 reruns.
labSteps: Inventory the DAG on paper first: list the 3 stages (Lakeflow pipeline → MDM golden refresh → gold marts/KPI refresh) and draw the dependency edges + which KPIs each stage feeds. Write the intended 8am freshness SLA in your RUNBOOK as the target you'll alert on.

Create the Job with a **pipeline task** that runs your W33 Lakeflow declarative pipeline (select the existing pipeline; full-refresh=false). Confirm it runs green on its own before adding anything downstream.

Add task 2 (MDM golden-record refresh notebook/SQL) with `depends_on` = the pipeline task, and task 3 (gold marts + KPI refresh) depending on task 2. Set task 3's `run_if = ALL_SUCCESS` so it never publishes off a half-built silver/MDM layer.

Add reliability controls to each task: `max_retries` (2) with a `min_retry_interval_millis`, a `timeout_seconds` sized to ~1.5x normal runtime, and set the job `max_concurrent_runs = 1`. Add a job-level `run_date` and `env` parameter and read them inside the MDM/gold tasks (TODO markers in the scaffold) instead of hard-coding.

Pass state between tasks with `taskValues`: have the MDM task set `providers_collapsed` and `records_quarantined`, and have the gold/KPI task read them to stamp the run's KPI row (so lineage of counts flows through the DAG, not a shared side table).

Wire notifications: on-failure to your email + a webhook system destination, AND add an on-duration-threshold-exceeded alert set to your 8am-SLA budget. Set a cron schedule (nightly, correct timezone) but leave it PAUSED for the lab.

Break it on purpose: add a temporary `assert False` (or a bad cast) in the MDM task, trigger the run, and watch (a) the automatic retries exhaust, (b) the on-failure alert fire, (c) task 3 stay skipped because ALL_SUCCESS wasn't met. Screenshot the run timeline.

Recover cleanly: remove the injected failure, use **Repair Run** to resume from the failed MDM task (NOT a full rerun), and confirm only the failed + downstream tasks re-execute. Note in the RUNBOOK the exact repair procedure.

Prove idempotency: trigger the full Job 10x and record gold row counts + the 4 KPIs after each run; they must be stable (MERGE/overwrite-by-key, not append). Read the Gantt to find the single longest task and note it as next week's optimization candidate in Performance Notes.

liveMisconception: "If each task succeeds, the pipeline is correct." Untrue — order and gating are the product. Implement an audit-log Delta table that writes EXACTLY one row per pipeline run (run_id, job/task, started_at, ended_at, rows_in, rows_out, rows_quarantined, pass_rate, source_file_watermark, status) sourced from job run context and the Lakeflow event log; prove idempotency by re-running and confirming no duplicate audit rows.

Trace end-to-end table- and column-level lineage in Unity Catalog from bronze ingest through silver/MDM to a gold KPI, and produce a screenshot + written note identifying every downstream consumer of a PHI-adjacent column.

Configure Databricks SQL alerts and Databricks Jobs notifications that fire on (a) quarantine-rate threshold breach and (b) job/task failure, routed to email/webhook with a runbook link in the alert body.
Author a RUNBOOK covering operate + recover, including a step-by-step Delta time-travel RESTORE procedure that logs the recovery as its own audit-log row.
lessons: Observability pillars for data products: SLI vs SLO vs SLA, and the four data-specific signals (freshness, volume, quality, lineage). Framed to Maria: a stale or silently-broken price file means the hospital bills against wrong transparency data - a compliance and revenue-integrity risk, so 'silent is worse than loud.'

The audit-log pattern - one row per run. Where run metadata actually comes from: Databricks Jobs run/task context and task values, dbutils job metadata, the Lakeflow (DLT) event_log, and Unity Catalog system tables (system.lakeflow, system.access). Why the audit table must be written idempotently (MERGE on run_id) so retries never double-count.

Unity Catalog lineage and governance: automatic table + column lineage capture, reading lineage via Catalog Explorer and system.access.column_lineage / information_schema, and using lineage to answer 'who consumes this PHI-adjacent column downstream' for the masking/compliance story.

Turning signals into action: Databricks SQL dashboards for the KPI + SLA panel, Databricks SQL Alerts on threshold queries, Lakehouse Monitoring for data-quality/freshness profiling and drift, and Jobs notifications (on_failure / on_duration_warning) with webhook destinations.

Runbook discipline: severity levels, ownership/on-call, standard operate procedures, and recovery playbooks - including Delta time travel (DESCRIBE HISTORY) and RESTORE TABLE for clean rollback, plus the VACUUM retention caution that can silently make time-travel restore impossible.
businessFraming: Maria's team bills and audits against the CMS price-transparency data your pipeline serves; if a nightly load lands late, half-loaded, or silently drops rows, the hospital acts on wrong prices - a direct compliance-exposure and revenue-integrity risk. This week you stop trusting that the pipeline 'ran' and start proving it met a freshness and quality SLA, leaving one auditable row per run and an alert the moment it breaches.
labSummary: Instrument the Phase 2 medallion pipeline for production observability: compute freshness/quality/quarantine SLAs into a metrics Delta table, write a strictly one-row-per-run audit log via idempotent MERGE, wire Databricks SQL alerts and Jobs failure notifications to thresholds, capture Unity Catalog column lineage for a PHI-adjacent field, build a small SLA/KPI dashboard, and write the RUNBOOK that closes the loop with a rehearsed time-travel RESTORE. This lab operates on your OWN project tables - you are not ingesting new raw data, you are making the existing platform observable and recoverable.
labSteps: 1. Create an observability schema in Unity Catalog (e.g. ops.audit_log and ops.sla_metrics) with explicit typed schemas. Define your SLA thresholds as a small config table or dict: freshness_max_minutes, min_pricing_completeness_pass_rate, max_quarantine_rate, and a duplicate-collapse target. Write the numeric targets down - they are the contract the rest of the lab tests against.

2. At the end of the silver/gold job, capture run context (run_id, job_id, task, start/end timestamps) and compute this run's metrics: rows_in, rows_out, rows_quarantined, pricing-completeness pass rate, duplicates collapsed, and freshness = now minus max source-file arrival watermark. Emit one metric-set for the run.

3. Write the audit row with an idempotent MERGE keyed on run_id (never a blind append) so a retried or 10x-replayed job produces zero duplicate audit rows. Re-run the job 3-5 times and query the table to prove the count is stable - this is your break-safely receipt.

4. Cross-check your hand-built audit numbers against the Lakeflow pipeline event_log (row counts, expectation pass/fail) and the Unity Catalog system tables (system.lakeflow.pipelines / system.access) so your audit log agrees with the platform's own telemetry; note any discrepancy in the architecture doc.

5. In Catalog Explorer, open the lineage graph for the gold KPI table and drill to column lineage on a PHI-adjacent field (e.g. provider/NPI or organization name). Screenshot the upstream-to-downstream path and list every downstream consumer; save this as the governance evidence for the masking story.

6. Build a Databricks SQL dashboard with a query over ops.sla_metrics: current freshness, pass rate, quarantine rate vs their thresholds (green/red), plus a 30-run trend. This is the single pane Maria's lead would glance at each morning.

7. Create a Databricks SQL Alert on the quarantine-rate query (trigger when max quarantine_rate over the last run > threshold) and add Jobs notifications on_failure / on_duration_warning routed to email or a webhook. Force a breach (feed a deliberately dirty batch) and confirm the alert actually fires; capture the alert message.

8. Rehearse recovery: run DESCRIBE HISTORY on a gold table, pick a known-good version, RESTORE TABLE ... VERSION AS OF, and write a NEW audit-log row recording the restore (who/when/from-version/why). Confirm the KPI returns to correct values.

9. Write the RUNBOOK: SLA table, alert-to-action mapping, severity levels, the operate checklist, and the numbered recovery playbook (quarantine spike, late/failed load, bad-data rollback via time travel) - including the VACUUM retention caution. Add a 'Performance/Ops Notes' entry: what you now detect that was previously silent, with a before/after.

title: Git deep — branching, PRs & code review for data
objectives: Configure Databricks Git folders (Repos) against a GitHub remote so 100% of the running project's notebooks and config live as notebooks-as-code, and demonstrate a full clone -> edit -> commit -> push cycle with zero edits made outside the repo.

Execute a short-lived feature-branch workflow (branch -> commit -> PR -> review -> merge) for a real change to the silver-layer validation logic, keeping main continuously deployable and mapping the dev branch to the dev Unity Catalog.

Author a PR whose description IS a decision log (what changed, why, blast radius, rollback) and run a data-specific code review that catches at least 3 risk classes: a grain/schema change, a non-idempotent write, and a silent-failure/quality regression.

Reproduce the 'manual workspace change lost on deploy' trap end to end, then write the root-cause note and the Git guardrail (branch protection + CODEOWNERS + no-hotfix rule) that prevents PHI-masking or validation drift from being silently overwritten.
Configure branch protection and a CODEOWNERS map so critical paths (silver validation, masking, MDM merge) require review before merge to main.
lessons: Notebooks-as-code & Databricks Git folders (Repos): how a notebook serializes to source (the '# Databricks notebook source' .py format), why the interactive workspace is NOT a source of truth, Git folders vs Workspace files, and supported Git providers/auth (PAT, service principal). The mental shift: your pipeline is code in a repo, not clicks in a UI. (~55 min)

A branching model for data teams: trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches vs heavyweight GitFlow, why data code favors small trunk-based changes, and environment mapping (feature/dev branch -> dev catalog, main -> prod catalog) so a branch has a safe place to run. Why 'main is always deployable' matters more when a bad merge can corrupt a stateful table. (~50 min)

Pull requests as decision logs: PR anatomy, keeping PRs small and reviewable, linking each PR back to the Architecture Doc / Charter, and writing the 'why' so the PR becomes an interview answer later. Specific beats generic; documentation = interview prep, prove a human did the work. (~40 min)

Code review FOR DATA (recognition before evaluation): a review checklist that a generic software checklist misses -- did the grain/primary key change? is the write idempotent (MERGE/overwrite by key, not append)? did a quality expectation get loosened or a quarantine path get silenced? does it read/write the right catalog? are secrets or PHI columns exposed? Reviewing for 'breaks safely, not silently.' (~45 min)

The 'manual workspace change lost on deploy' trap: how drift opens up when someone hotfixes a notebook in the workspace UI, how the next Git deploy overwrites it, and why on PHI-adjacent data a lost masking hotfix is a compliance incident. The discipline: every change is a branch + PR; the workspace is disposable. Warn against AI over-engineering the repo (over-modularized files, needless indirection) -- be the human in the loop. (~40 min)
businessFraming: In week 37 you made the pipeline observable; now make it safe to CHANGE. Last sprint an analyst hotfixed the PHI-masking cell directly in the Databricks workspace to patch a leaking column, then the nightly deploy re-pushed the old notebook and silently re-exposed provider tax IDs -- a reportable compliance event and hours of Maria's team unable to trust the pricing mart. A real Git workflow (branches, reviewed PRs, protected main) is the control that makes every change to PHI-adjacent code traceable, reviewable, and impossible to lose on deploy.
labSummary: Put the entire Phase 2 'Provider Pricing Integrity' pipeline under a real Git workflow: connect it as a Databricks Git folder backed by a GitHub repo, make a schema-touching change to silver validation on a feature branch, open a decision-log PR, run a data-specific review that catches three planted risks, then deliberately reproduce and remediate the 'manual change lost on deploy' trap. You end with branch protection + CODEOWNERS guarding the critical paths and a written root-cause note.
labSteps: Create a GitHub repo for the project and connect it as a Databricks Git folder (Repos): commit the existing Phase 2 notebooks + config as notebooks-as-code on main. Verify the '# Databricks notebook source' .py serialization by viewing the raw files in GitHub -- confirm nothing lives only in the workspace UI.

Establish the branching + environment map: protect main, create a feature branch (feature/silver-npi-normalization), and confirm the branch runs against the DEV Unity Catalog (dev.silver) not prod. Document the branch->catalog mapping in the Architecture Doc.

Make one real, grain-touching change on the branch: tighten the silver NPPES validation (e.g., normalize/validate NPI as the composite key and add a Lakeflow expectation). Commit in small, well-messaged commits that reference the change's 'why'.

Plant three review targets to exercise the checklist: (a) a commit that changes the primary/merge key, (b) a commit that switches a Delta write from MERGE-by-key to append (non-idempotent), (c) a commit that loosens a data-quality expectation / silences a quarantine path. These simulate what a reviewer must catch.

Open a Pull Request whose body is a decision log: what changed, why, grain/schema impact, idempotency proof (rerun 10x -> row counts stable), quality/quarantine impact, and rollback plan (Delta time travel version). Link the PR to the Charter/Architecture Doc.

Run the data code review AS the reviewer using the checklist from lesson 4: comment on each of the three planted risks, request changes, and resolve them on the branch. Capture the review thread as evidence a human reviewed it.

Reproduce the trap: make a 'hotfix' edit directly in the workspace UI (outside the repo), then pull/redeploy from Git and watch the workspace edit get overwritten and lost. Screenshot before/after and write the 2-4 sentence root-cause note.

Remediate: add branch protection (require PR + 1 approval, no direct pushes to main) and a CODEOWNERS file mapping silver-validation, masking, and MDM-merge paths to a required reviewer. Re-attempt a direct push to main and confirm it is now blocked. Update the Runbook with the 'no workspace hotfixes -- branch + PR only' rule.
Merge the reviewed PR to main and confirm the change lands in dev; leave promotion-to-prod for the W39 CI/CD week (do not build the pipeline yet).

title: Databricks Asset Bundles (DABs) & infrastructure-as-code
objectives: Given the running Provider Pricing Integrity project, author a databricks.yml bundle that declares the Lakeflow pipeline, the orchestration Job, cluster/serverless config, and permissions as code, and validate it with `databricks bundle validate` returning zero errors.

Configure at least two named targets (dev and prod) with per-environment overrides (catalog/schema, cluster size, schedule pause status, run-as identity) so the SAME source deploys to both with no hand edits — prove it by diffing the two resolved configs.

Deploy the bundle to a dev target with `databricks bundle deploy` and confirm zero manual drift: every job, pipeline, and grant that exists in the workspace was created by the bundle, verified against a pre-deploy inventory.

Use bundle variables and `${workspace...}`/`${resources...}` substitutions plus dev-mode name prefixing so parallel developer deployments never collide, demonstrated by two dev deploys producing isolated, prefixed resources.
Wire the W39 GitHub Actions CI/CD to run `bundle validate` on PR and `bundle deploy --target prod` on merge using a service principal, so a merge promotes dev→prod by code with an auditable run link.
lessons: Why IaC for a data platform: click-ops drift is the silent failure. What 'the workspace is the source of truth' costs you (un-reviewable changes, un-reproducible prod, no rollback) vs. 'Git is the source of truth.' Where DABs sits relative to Terraform — DABs wraps the Databricks Terraform provider for Databricks-native assets (jobs, pipelines, grants, notebooks), so you get declarative deploys without writing HCL. (~1.5h)

Anatomy of a bundle: the databricks.yml root — `bundle` (name), `include` globs, `variables`, `artifacts`, `resources` (jobs, pipelines, schemas, grants, volumes), and `targets`. How resources map to real workspace objects, and how deploy is a plan/apply that reconciles state, not an append. (~2h)

Targets & environment parametrization: dev vs. prod as named targets; `mode: development` (name-prefixing, paused schedules, single-node concurrency safety) vs. `mode: production` (locked run-as, no prefixing, enforced deployment path). Per-target overrides for catalog/schema, cluster or serverless config, and run-as service principal. Substitutions and variables so nothing is hard-coded. (~2.5h)

Identity, permissions, and the prod deploy: service principals vs. user tokens, `run_as`, and declaring `permissions`/Unity Catalog `grants` in the bundle so access is reviewed in Git, not clicked. Why prod must deploy as a service principal (auditability, no personal-token blast radius) — this sets up W41 governance. (~1.5h)

Operating bundles safely: `validate` → `deploy` → `run`, reading the deploy plan, `bundle summary`, and `bundle destroy` for teardown. State locking, the `.databricks/bundle` state, and what happens when the workspace drifts from code (and how to detect it). (~1h)
businessFraming: Maria's revenue-cycle team now depends on the pricing-integrity pipeline for the 8am completeness report, but today it only exists because someone clicked it into the dev workspace — there is no reviewed, reproducible way to stand up prod, and a hotfix applied by hand in one environment silently diverges from the other. For PHI-adjacent pricing data, an un-auditable, un-reproducible deployment is a compliance and continuity risk: if the workspace is lost or a bad manual change breaks the SLA, there is no rollback and no record of who changed what. Packaging the whole project as infrastructure-as-code turns "it works on my workspace" into "any environment is one reviewed command away," which is what makes the platform trustworthy to the business.
labSummary: Take the ENTIRE Provider Pricing Integrity project — the Lakeflow declarative pipeline, the Databricks Job that orchestrates ingest→bronze→silver→MDM→gold, its cluster/serverless config, and its Unity Catalog grants — and express all of it as a single Databricks Asset Bundle. Define dev and prod targets with per-environment config, deploy to dev with zero manual drift, prove two developers can deploy in parallel without collision, and hand the prod deploy off to the W39 GitHub Actions workflow running as a service principal so a merge to main promotes the change by code with an auditable run link. No new raw data this week — you are IaC-ifying the platform you already built.
labSteps: Inventory first (measure before you change): install/authenticate the Databricks CLI, then snapshot what exists today — `databricks jobs list`, `databricks pipelines list`, and the UC grants on your project schema — into a `pre_deploy_inventory.md`. This is your drift baseline; the acceptance test compares against it.

Scaffold the bundle: run `databricks bundle init` (default-python or an empty template), then replace the generated resources so `databricks.yml` declares your project's `bundle.name`, an `include` for resource files, and a `resources` block referencing your existing Lakeflow pipeline definition and Job. Keep source notebooks/py files where they are; the bundle points at them, it does not rewrite them.

Parametrize with variables and substitutions: add a `variables` block (catalog, schema/prefix, warehouse or cluster size, notification email) and replace every hard-coded catalog/schema/path in the resource definitions with `${var.*}` and `${workspace.*}` references. Nothing environment-specific should be a literal.

Define targets: create a `dev` target with `mode: development` (auto name-prefixing, paused schedule, your user as run-as) and a `prod` target with `mode: production`, a service-principal `run_as`, the prod catalog/schema, production cluster/serverless sizing, and an active schedule. Set `default: true` on dev.

Validate and diff environments: run `databricks bundle validate` until it returns zero errors, then run `databricks bundle validate -o json --target dev` vs. `--target prod` and diff the resolved configs to PROVE the same source yields two correct, isolated environments (different catalog, run-as, schedule state, cluster size).

Deploy to dev and confirm zero drift: `databricks bundle deploy --target dev`, then `databricks bundle summary`. Re-list jobs/pipelines/grants and diff against `pre_deploy_inventory.md` — every project object in the workspace must now be bundle-managed (dev-prefixed), with nothing orphaned or hand-created. Trigger `databricks bundle run <job_key>` and confirm the pipeline executes.

Prove collision-free parallel dev: from a second identity or with `DATABRICKS_BUNDLE_ENV`/a second `--target`, deploy again and show the dev-mode name prefix isolates the two deployments (two `[dev you] provider_pricing_job` vs. `[dev teammate] ...`) with no shared-object clobbering.

Wire prod into W39 CI/CD: extend the existing GitHub Actions workflow so PRs run `databricks bundle validate` (fail the check on errors) and merge-to-main runs `databricks bundle deploy --target prod` authenticated as a service principal via OIDC or a stored secret. Open a trivial PR (e.g., bump a variable default), let it deploy prod, and capture the Actions run URL.

Break-and-recover drill + write the 'why': manually edit the deployed dev job in the UI (change its schedule), re-run `databricks bundle deploy`, and observe the bundle reconcile the drift back to code. Record before/after and write a 1-paragraph decision note on why Git-is-source-of-truth beats click-ops for a compliance-sensitive pipeline.

title: Governance & Security — PHI, RBAC, Masking & Service Principals

Implement Unity Catalog column masks and row filters so that the `analyst` persona sees hashed/redacted provider identifiers and only their in-scope hospital rows, while the `engineer` persona sees cleartext for debugging — verified by querying the SAME table as each principal and diffing the output.

Design and apply an RBAC model with account groups (analyst vs engineer) and the three-level GRANT chain (USE CATALOG → USE SCHEMA → SELECT), demonstrating least privilege by proving an analyst is DENIED on bronze/quarantine and on masking UDFs.

Replace every personal PAT in the project's Jobs and DABs with a service principal that owns the pipeline run, and prove the job succeeds under the SP identity with only the grants it needs (no ALL PRIVILEGES).

Query Unity Catalog system tables (system.access.audit, system.access.column_lineage) to produce an evidence artifact answering 'who read the NPI column, when, and were they masked' — the auditable compliance story a HIPAA reviewer would ask for.

Unity Catalog's governance model end to end: the securable hierarchy (metastore → catalog → schema → table/view/function), account-level groups vs workspace-local, ownership, and the three-level privilege chain (USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA/SELECT) — why a SELECT grant alone silently fails. Contrast the modern approach with legacy Hive-metastore ACLs so the learner can defend the choice. (~1.5 hrs)

When to mask vs when to physically separate into a restricted schema. (~1.5 hrs)

Machine identity for production: service principals vs personal access tokens, why 'the pipeline should not run as a human' (offboarding risk, audit ambiguity, token sprawl), OAuth machine-to-machine (M2M) client credentials, run-as identity on Jobs, and the least-privilege grant set a pipeline SP actually needs. (~1.25 hrs)

Auditability as a deliverable: Unity Catalog system tables (system.access.audit, table/column lineage), what events are captured, retention, and how to turn a raw audit log into a one-page 'access evidence' answer — because in an interview and in a real audit, 'prove it' beats 'we masked it'. (~1.0 hr)

A single over-broad grant or a personal token baked into a job is the exact finding that fails a payer audit or a HIPAA risk assessment, and 'we trusted people not to look' is not a control. This week converts the pipeline from 'works' into 'defensible': who can see what, why, and can you prove it.

Every control is verified by querying as each persona and diffing — a control you cannot demonstrate does not exist.
labSteps: Classify first. Create `governance.data_classification` (column, table, sensitivity_level, rule, rationale) and populate it for every silver/gold column touching NPI, provider_name, tin, address, hospital_id. This table is the single source of truth that drives every mask below — recognition before evaluation, and your written 'why'.

Stand up personas. Create two account groups, `ppi_analysts` and `ppi_engineers`, and add yourself to each via separate test principals (or use is_account_group_member() with a swappable test group). Document in the runbook which real-world role each maps to.

Grant least privilege. Write the three-level GRANT chain so analysts get USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT on the gold marts ONLY; engineers additionally get SELECT on silver and bronze/quarantine. Prove least privilege: run a SELECT on `bronze.raw_pricing` as an analyst and capture the PERMISSION_DENIED error as evidence.

Mask sensitive columns. Create UC SQL UDF masks: sha2(npi,256) and sha2(tin,256) for analysts, cleartext for engineers via is_account_group_member('ppi_engineers'); redact street address to ZIP-only. ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK on the gold provider mart. Verify by SELECTing the same rows as each persona and diffing the two result sets.

Filter rows. Create a row-filter UDF so `ppi_analysts` see only rows whose hospital_id is in an assignment table (governance.analyst_scope), while engineers see all rows. Apply with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER and verify row counts differ by persona. Confirm masks + filter compose (an analyst gets fewer rows AND hashed IDs).

Idempotency + recovery check. Re-run the entire policy notebook a second and third time; confirm CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION and SET MASK are idempotent (no duplicate policies, no drift). Note in the runbook how to remove a mask (UNSET MASK) for an emergency break-glass, and who authorizes it.

Kill the personal token. Create a service principal, grant it exactly the pipeline's needs (USE on catalog/schema, SELECT/MODIFY on the tables it writes, no ALL PRIVILEGES), set the Job/DAB run-as to the SP, and configure OAuth M2M so no PAT is stored. Trigger the job and confirm it runs as the SP identity.

Prove it with audit. Query system.access.audit filtered to your catalog for the last day: show the analyst's masked SELECT, the denied bronze read, and the SP-run job. Join to column lineage to answer 'who read npi and were they masked'. Export a one-page 'Access Evidence' summary into the RUNBOOK.

Write the why. Add a 'Security & Governance Decisions' section to the ARCHITECTURE DOC: why hashing over tokenization here, why masks over separate restricted tables, why an SP over a PAT, and the one control you deliberately did NOT add and why (scope discipline — avoid over-engineering).

-- Idempotent: safe to re-run. CREATE OR REPLACE + SET MASK do not stack.
-- Prereq: catalog/schema from Phase 2 already exist under Unity Catalog.

-- 0) Config -----------------------------------------------------------------

-- 1) Column mask: cleartext for engineers, hash for everyone else ----------
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION governance.mask_identifier(id STRING)
RETURN CASE
  -- TODO: replace group literal with your engineer group name
  WHEN is_account_group_member('ppi_engineers') THEN id
  -- TODO: decide hash vs redaction vs tokenization and justify in ARCH doc
  ELSE sha2(id, 256)
END;

-- TODO: create a second mask for address -> ZIP-only (redaction pattern)
-- CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION governance.mask_address(addr STRING) RETURN ...;

-- 2) Row filter: analysts limited to assigned hospitals --------------------
-- Assumes governance.analyst_scope(hospital_id) lists in-scope hospitals.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION governance.filter_by_scope(hospital_id STRING)
RETURN
  is_account_group_member('ppi_engineers')  -- engineers: all rows
  -- TODO: analysts -> only rows in governance.analyst_scope
  OR hospital_id IN (SELECT s.hospital_id FROM governance.analyst_scope s);

-- 3) Bind policies to the gold provider mart -------------------------------
-- TODO: point at YOUR gold table; add every column from data_classification
ALTER TABLE gold.provider_mart
  ALTER COLUMN npi SET MASK governance.mask_identifier;
-- TODO: ALTER COLUMN tin SET MASK governance.mask_identifier;
-- TODO: ALTER COLUMN address SET MASK governance.mask_address;
ALTER TABLE gold.provider_mart
  SET ROW FILTER governance.filter_by_scope ON (hospital_id);

-- 4) Verify (run interactively as each persona; do NOT skip) ---------------
-- As analyst:  SELECT npi, tin, address, hospital_id FROM gold.provider_mart LIMIT 20;
-- As engineer: SELECT npi, tin, address, hospital_id FROM gold.provider_mart LIMIT 20;
-- TODO: capture both outputs + row counts as your control evidence.

-- Break-glass (document who authorizes; do not leave applied):
-- ALTER TABLE gold.provider_mart ALTER COLUMN npi UNSET MASK;

From a clean checkout run `databricks bundle validate --target prod` and confirm every bundle resource resolves — the Lakeflow pipeline, the orchestrating Job, UC catalog/schema and grants, and the service principal run-as. Record the git SHA; do not deploy yet.

COLD-START DEPLOY: `databricks bundle deploy --target prod` into an empty prod-like workspace/schema so you prove nothing depends on hand-created state. Seed the Auto Loader landing volume with one fresh CMS Hospital Price Transparency file and emit one batch of provider-change events, then trigger the Job.

OBSERVE & PROVE QUALITY: watch the Lakeflow pipeline event log and expectation metrics; confirm the KPI mart lands inside the freshness SLA. Inject one deliberately malformed row and confirm it lands in quarantine WITH reason + timestamp and fires the alert — loud, not silent.

PROVE IDEMPOTENCY: re-drop the exact same CMS file and re-run the Job 3× (aim for your standing 10× discipline). Assert zero net change in silver/golden via the watermarked, composite-key MERGE — no duplicate providers, quarantine counts stable.

MEASURE FIRST, THEN TUNE: open the Spark UI / query profile for the slowest gold aggregation, identify the ONE bottleneck stage (skew, wide scan, or a big-vs-small join), apply exactly one fix (liquid clustering by query pattern / broadcast / repartition), and record before/after timing in Performance Notes led by the business outcome ("Maria's KPI mart now lands before 8am").

GOVERNANCE AUDIT: review UC grants against least-privilege, confirm PHI-adjacent columns are masked (column mask / row filter) for the analyst role, and capture a Catalog Explorer lineage view end-to-end for the architecture doc's governance section.

RECOVERY DRILL: simulate a bad load into the golden table, then restore it using ONLY runbook commands — `DESCRIBE HISTORY`, Delta time travel (`VERSION AS OF` / `RESTORE`) cross-checked against the audit log — and note the VACUUM retention that keeps the drill possible. Time the recovery and write it down.

CUT THE RELEASE: open the PR to `main`; GitHub Actions runs `bundle validate` → deploy to prod → smoke run as the service principal. On green, tag `v1.0.0` and confirm the Actions badge and job run history show the automated, run-as-SP execution.

ASSEMBLE & FRESH-EYES DRY RUN: finalize the README (architecture diagram, KPI table with real numbers, CI badge, links to charter / 4-part architecture doc / Performance Notes / runbook / decision log). Then have a peer (or yourself, cold) deploy and recover using only the runbook; fix any gap they hit and capture final SLA evidence.

datasets.whatsMessy: Rate-limited, paginated, occasionally-timing-out live endpoint used to feed / validate the provider-change event stream; production hardening means the streaming path must tolerate throttling and partial responses without breaking the watermarked dedup — a good place to prove the pipeline fails safely on a slow upstream.

mirrorNote: Do this whole integration on YOUR mirror project's stack, not Maria's. Pick the SLA and the failure that would actually cost your target industry money or trigger a regulator, and make the release prove it: SEC EDGAR filings landing before a market-open dashboard, NOAA weather feeds behind an operations alert, CoinGecko prices where a stale number misprices a position, or a ReliefWeb/data.gov feed a program officer reports upward. Your cold-start run, recovery drill, and Performance Notes headline should name your industry's deadline and dollar/risk outcome in the same specific, non-generic voice.
deliverable: A tagged release (v1.0.0) of Project 1 in GitHub: the project deployed to a prod target via a DAB promoted by a green GitHub Actions run executing as a service principal, PLUS the finalized living deliverables — the project charter, the updated 4-part architecture doc (governance/streaming/orchestration/CI-CD decisions filled in), a Performance Notes section with >=3 before/after tunings each led by a business outcome, a runbook with numbered deploy/backfill/quarantine-replay/time-travel-restore/alert-triage playbooks, and a README that makes the whole thing legible in a 30-second skim.
acceptance: Green-lit only if ALL hold: (1) a cold-start `bundle deploy` + Job run on a clean target produces gold KPIs within the stated freshness SLA with a captured expectation report; (2) an injected bad row is quarantined with reason + timestamp and fires an alert, and re-running the same file 3× yields zero net change; (3) the golden table is restored from a simulated bad load using only runbook commands (time travel + audit log) and the recovery time is recorded; (4) the GitHub Actions release run is green, ran as the service principal, and the git tag exists; (5) Performance Notes shows >=3 before/after tunings each leading with a business outcome; (6) a fresh reader can deploy and recover from the runbook alone, and PHI-adjacent columns are confirmed masked with end-to-end lineage visible in Catalog Explorer.
liveRecap: Screen-share your cold-start end-to-end run and the green GitHub Actions release: show the tag, the service-principal job run, the Lakeflow expectation report, and the KPI mart landing inside the freshness SLA. Then walk the 30-second GitHub skim of your README as if the reviewer is a hiring manager who will not scroll.
liveMisconception: \"It ran on my cluster, so it's production.\" A pipeline that only runs when you click it, under your personal token, with recovery steps that live in your head, is a demo — not a data product. Production means it deploys from a tag as a service principal, breaks loudly and reruns idempotently, and a stranger can operate and recover it from the runbook without you. The related trap: mistaking AI-style over-engineering (dozens of tiny files, needless abstraction) for senior work — reviewers read that as noise, not judgment.
liveHotSeat: Defend your release decisions: Why is your freshness SLA that number and not tighter or looser — what does Maria (or your mirror persona) actually lose when it slips? Walk us through your recovery drill: which Delta version did you restore to, how did the audit log confirm it, and what VACUUM retention keeps that recovery possible? Point to the ONE tuning in your Performance Notes and state its business outcome before the technical change. And which grant or mask would you tighten first if a PHI-adjacent column leaked to the analyst role tomorrow?
portfolio: Project 1 becomes the flagship: a public GitHub repo that reads as senior in 30 seconds — README with an architecture diagram, a KPI table carrying real before/after numbers, a CI badge on a green release, and one-click links to the charter, the 4-part architecture doc, Performance Notes, runbook, and a decision log where each production choice is written as an interview-ready answer. This is the artifact you point interviewers to in Phase 4.
